author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Letter from the Old World
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
The envelope was made from a page torn out of an old technical manual.

It arrived at Brasswatch Yard wrapped around a small packet of electrical connectors, delivered by a trader who did not know the sender's name. The paper had been folded so precisely that I could almost hear Danse correcting someone's technique.

He recognized the handwriting before he opened it.

His face went still.

"Haylen?"

I looked at the packet, then at him.

"Maybe."

He carried it into the workshop and shut the door. I stayed outside. It was not an act of generosity; it was an effort not to confuse my curiosity with his permission.

Five minutes passed.

Then ten.

At last, he opened the door.

"Jasper?"

I went inside.

Danse stood beside the bench with a folded note in one hand. The packet of connectors lay unopened. His shoulders were set as if he expected an inspection.

"It's from Haylen," he said.

"Do you want to tell me what it says?"

"Yes."

He handed me the paper.

The message was short. Haylen wrote that the Brotherhood had changed patrol routes near a settlement Danse once supplied. Some residents were afraid a former Paladin might try to use the settlement's old radio frequency. The letter did not ask Danse to return. It asked him to avoid the channel until the people who lived there had chosen a safer way to communicate.

At the end, in smaller writing, she'd added:

I HOPE YOU ARE WELL. PLEASE DON'T ANSWER THROUGH THE OLD NET.

I read it twice.

"She wants you safe," I said.

"She wants civilians safe."

"Both can be true."

Danse did not answer.

He took the note and placed it beside the purifier ledger.

"The old net is the most reliable frequency I know."

"That doesn't make it the right one."

"I know."

He sounded irritated.

"Danse."

"I know, Jasper."

He moved to the workbench and began sorting the connectors by size, though they were already sorted. The motion was familiar enough to make my chest ache.

I waited until he stopped.

"What are you afraid of?" I asked.

"That if I don't respond, she'll think I have forgotten her."

"And if you respond through the channel?"

"People could be endangered."

"Then the answer isn't a radio message."

He looked at me, the conflict plain.

"She's one of the few people who knew me before everything changed."

I stood beside him, close enough that our sleeves touched.

"You don't have to stop caring about her to respect the boundary she's giving you."

His breath caught.

"That's not what I meant."

"I know."

He looked down at his hands.

"I was trained to answer a call. Silence meant failure. Sometimes abandonment."

"Then maybe you need a different way to show you're still here."

He thought about it.

The following morning, we went to Neri with the note. Not to ask permission to answer Haylen, but to ask whether the Threadway courier network could deliver a sealed letter without identifying the settlement or exposing the person who had carried the first message.

Neri listened and shook their head.

"Not without the recipient agreeing to receive it."

Danse's jaw tightened.

"Then how do people communicate across the doors?"

"They arrange it," Neri said. "Or they wait."

"Waiting is unreliable."

"Sometimes it is the only honest answer."

He looked as though he wanted to argue. Instead, he asked for a blank page.

We returned to Brasswatch.

He wrote the letter slowly. I did not read over his shoulder. When he finished, he folded it and placed it in a plain envelope with no identifying marks on the outside.

He told me what he'd written only after he sealed it.

He had thanked Haylen for the warning. He had said he would not use the old network. He had told her that his life was different, and that the people who once served beside him still mattered. He had not asked her to put herself at risk for a reply.

"And now?" I asked.

"Now I wait until there's a safe invitation."

He looked almost ill from the effort.

I found two cups and poured water from the safe hand pump.

"That sounds difficult."

"It is."

"Welcome to the club."

He took the cup.

"You make light of everything."

"Not everything. Just the parts that might crush us if we never laugh."

A small smile reached his mouth.

We worked the rest of the day on the purifier's intake pipe. Severus had warned us about residues that appeared after the system sat idle. Danse had taken the criticism seriously enough to redesign the testing schedule. Every sample would be collected and labeled before anyone declared the water safe.

At noon, Tamsin stopped by with a list of residents who needed deliveries until the repairs were complete. Danse read the list carefully.

"Three households require assistance carrying water," he said.

"Four," I corrected. "One person doesn't want their name announced publicly."

He looked up.

"Then we can arrange a route without displaying it."

I smiled.

"You're learning."

"I was already capable of discretion."

"Understatement of the century."

He shook his head, but there was warmth in it.

The letter stayed in a locked drawer. Not because he had stopped wanting to send it, but because wanting didn't give him the right to use a channel that might harm someone else.

That evening he found me on the workshop steps.

"Could I ask you something?" he said.

"Always."

He sat beside me, the old scarf loose around his neck.

"Do you think caring about someone far away makes what I have with you less important?"

I turned toward him.

"No. You know what I believe about loving more than one person. But even outside romance, care isn't a resource we use up by remembering people."

He nodded slowly.

"I still have trouble believing that."

"I know."

"Then perhaps I should say something I do believe." He looked directly at me. "I want you here tonight. Not because Haylen isn't here. Because you are."

Warmth settled behind my ribs.

"That I can do."

He touched my cheek with one hand, waiting for the small answering movement that told him I wanted the kiss. I leaned into his palm.

His mouth was warm. His beard scratched lightly against my skin. He was still learning how to be gentle without making gentleness feel like a protocol.

When we parted, he kept his forehead against mine for a moment.

"Thank you," he said.

"For what?"

"For not asking me to forget."

I squeezed his hand.

The next morning, the letter was still in the drawer.

The purifier was still offline.

Both were unfinished.

For the first time, Danse seemed willing to let unfinished mean that he could keep caring without taking the wrong action simply to make the waiting stop.
